clue.text: Second summer extra-blue?

parts.note: read as one who sums, an adder, not the season

explanation.surface: Someone describes the second month of summer as a deeper blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer' looks like the season but is a person who sums figures, an ADDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue means unhappy, so a more extreme blue mood is a gloomier one: a comparative of low spirits.

clue.text: Region accommodates new stadium

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, so the region word holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: a region is an area

explanation.surface: A district makes room for a newly built sports ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A stadium is an enclosed space for sport or spectacle, the modern sense of the Roman amphitheatre floor.

clue.text: Inset days arranged in lines

indicators.note: arranged tells us the letters of the two words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Days set into a calendar are laid out in rows.
explanation.definitionFit: A line can mean a family succession, so ruling houses passing power down generations are royal lines.

clue.text: Before being collared by extremist, look again at manifesto?

indicators.note: being collared means being held round the neck, so the extremist word wraps round the earlier one

parts.note: rad is short for radical, an extremist
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: A political radical gets a second look at a party manifesto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manifesto?' adds a playful example of something one might study a second time; the definition is really 'look again at'.
explanation.definitionFit: To go over a text a second time is to study it once more, as one might a policy document.

clue.text: Government to fail — team out in reshuffle, one by no means partisan

indicators.note: out says some letters are taken away and reshuffle says the rest of the phrase is rearranged

parts.note: a team is a group of men, a set of players

explanation.surface: A government falls after its cabinet team is sacked in a reshuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of GOVERNMENT TO FAIL, remove MEN ('team'), and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: An elector with no fixed party loyalty is the archetypal non-partisan in an election.

clue.text: Crewman's in, knowing about foot and sore heel, to react angrily

parts.note: fly is British slang for knowing or sharp
of can mean about, as in 'speak of'

indicators.note: in says the crewman goes inside the rearranged letters
sore here means troubled or disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: a hand is a member of a ship's crew; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A sailor with a bad foot and sore heel, in the know, loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knowing' is British slang FLY, not wisdom; 'sore' scrambles FT and HEEL, and 'in' puts the crewman inside that jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from an axe head flying loose: it means losing one's temper suddenly.

clue.text: Is wholly incongruous with wise or solemn manner

indicators.note: incongruous means out of place, so the letters are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Something is entirely out of keeping with a grave, sage demeanour.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls are proverbially wise and grave-looking, so behaving like one is solemn and sage.

clue.text: Route reportedly found by traveller down in London?

definitions.meaning: route said aloud is root, and a potato is a swollen root
a whimsical word for someone who rides the London Underground, which runs down below the streets

explanation.surface: A route is found by someone travelling on London's Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: London's Underground railway is called the Tube, so its passengers can be playfully named after it; 'down' because the trains run below ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A swollen underground plant stem stores food like a root, and a Tube rider is one in the jokey sense.

clue.text: Collapse under thing roaming in gloaming

indicators.note: in a down answer, under puts the collapse word below the other piece
roaming means wandering, so the letters of thing wander into a new order

parts.note: to collapse is to fall

explanation.surface: Something drifting about in the dusk collapses.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloaming is a Scottish word for dusk, the time when dark comes on.

clue.text: Mint coin

parts.note: a penny is a coin
a royal was an old English gold coin

explanation.surface: A newly minted coin, straight from the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' looks like a description of a coin in perfect condition; it is the herb. 'coin' supplies two coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennyroyal is a small aromatic plant of the mint family, once used in folk medicine.

clue.text: Year at Slough is thing feared

indicators.note: at means next to, so the year letter sits beside the swamp word

parts.note: a slough is a swamp or bog

explanation.surface: A year spent in the town of Slough is something to dread.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London often mocked as dreary, but here it is a swamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A bogy is a goblin or imaginary terror, something people dread.

clue.text: Disreputable knight's man on river …

indicators.note: in an across answer, on puts the man word after the river

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
to man is to staff

explanation.surface: A shady knight's servant stands on a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' looks like a noun for the knight's servant but is the verb to staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's fat, boastful, roguish knight.

clue.text: … right to have hard feelings about water pixie

indicators.note: about means around, so the feelings word goes round the letter for right

parts.note: spite is malicious resentment

explanation.surface: A water pixie is entitled to bear a grudge.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprite is a fairy or elf; water sprites are a folklore type of spirit.

clue.text: Beastie in town? On the contrary

indicators.note: in names one word lying within another, here run backwards by the next phrase
on the contrary swaps the roles, so the town is inside the beastie rather than the reverse

explanation.surface: A small creature loose in a town, or is it the other way round?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'town in Beastie': the letters sit in bEASTIe.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a town in Piedmont, Italy, famous for sparkling wine.

clue.text: 20 job gives result

parts.note: a score is twenty
a line is a line of work, a job

explanation.surface: A clue number pointing elsewhere produces an outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' looks like a cross-reference to another clue but is simply the number, a score.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport the final tally of goals or points shows the outcome of a match.

clue.text: Way to swell the public purse?

definitions.text: Way to swell the public purse?

parts.words: Way to swell the public purse?
parts.note: reads like a method of raising revenue, but way is a literal road that charges drivers to use it

explanation.definitionFit: A road charging a fee for use raises money, so it is a route that funds the treasury.

clue.text: MI6, appreciated in Division, finds proof

indicators.note: in says the agency and thanks go inside the division word

parts.note: a rent is a split or tear
SIS, the Secret Intelligence Service, is Britain's foreign spy agency, known as MI6
ta is British informal thanks

explanation.surface: The spy agency, valued within its division, comes up with evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proof' looks like evidence but is the suffix sense, as in waterproof.
explanation.definitionFit: Proof as in waterproof or bulletproof means able to withstand something.

clue.text: Pound caught with sister — that's the gossip

parts.note: a quid is British slang for a pound
a sister is a nun
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A pound is taken with a sister, so goes the rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: A quidnunc is a busybody, someone always asking what's new; the Latin means 'what now?'.

clue.text: Ingredient in Chinese cases you busted open

indicators.note: busted open means broken apart, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Food parcels in a Chinese meal are split open by you.
explanation.definitionFit: A salty condiment from fermented beans is a staple flavouring of Chinese cooking.

clue.text: Pride Gerard restored against second German XI

indicators.note: against means next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: elf is German for eleven

indicators.note: restored means put back together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Gerard, back in the side, plays against a German reserve eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'XI' looks like a football team but is the number eleven, ELF in German.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-regard is esteem for oneself, a form of vanity or conceit.

clue.text: Putting up painting on wall area causes commotion

indicators.note: in a down answer, putting up means writing the word upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a mural is a wall painting

explanation.surface: Hanging a fresco in a public area stirs up a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarum is an archaic word for an alarm or call to arms, hence a tumult.

clue.text: See 19
Last word to daughter is correct

parts.note: amen is the word said at the end of a prayer

explanation.surface: Having the last word with one's daughter is the right thing.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend is to correct or improve, as with a text.

clue.text: Everyone being rude but sailor making suggestion?

parts.note: everyone means all

indicators.note: but means except, so the sailor letters are dropped

parts.note: abusive means insulting or rude
AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: Everyone is offensive except a sailor making a proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' removes AB from ABUSIVE, leaving USIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusive speech works by hints and indirect reference rather than stating things outright.

clue.text: See 5Across
Store room in Escot House

indicators.note: to house is to contain, so the phrase holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: A storeroom inside a Devon country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Escot House is a country estate in East Devon; the letters sit in rooM IN Escot.
explanation.definitionFit: A mine of information is a rich store or supply.

clue.text: Wobbling n-nude parts we cover and support

indicators.note: wobbling means shaking unsteadily, so the letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: A stammering speaker's undergarments announce their job of covering wobbling bare bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefs or knickers are worn to cover and hold up the body's private parts.

clue.text: Males to bed ace Indy compiler — why no sex?

indicators.note: to bed is to embed, so the other pieces go inside the males

parts.note: he is a male, so two males give two copies
A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
Dac is a setter for the Independent newspaper, known as the Indy

explanation.surface: Men take a star Independent setter to bed, then ask why there's no sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the classic excuse, 'Not tonight, I've got a...'.
explanation.definitionFit: A throbbing head is the stock excuse for refusing intimacy.

clue.text: Victor, old player from United, runs into friend

indicators.note: into says those letters go inside the friend word

parts.note: mate is another word for friend
U is the abbreviation for United in football team names
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Victor, a veteran footballer from United, bumps into a pal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'player' looks like a footballer but is an actor: Victor Mature starred in Hollywood epics.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Mature was a 1940s-50s Hollywood actor, so an old stage or screen performer.
